section.content: Aspects of the present disclosure relate to machine learning instantiation in which an instance of an agent (e.g., including processing user input by a machine learning model to generate model output) is packaged as an agent object. In an example, the agent object is stored as a file, document, database, and/or the like. The agent object includes a role definition and/or an object embedded memory to define various aspects of the agent. Thus, the agent object allows portability of the agent, e.g., between users, across contexts, and/or for various subsequent processes, etc.
本公开的各方面涉及机器学习实例化，其中智能体的实例(例如，包括由机器学习模型处理用户输入以生成模型输出)被封装为智能体对象。在示例中，智能体对象被存储为文件、文档和/或数据库等。智能体对象包括角色定义和/或对象嵌入存储器，从而定义智能体的各个方面。因此，智能体对象允许智能体的可移植性，例如在用户之间、跨上下文和/或用于各种后续处理等。

Machine learning instantiationBackground

The machine learning model may be stateless such that the machine learning model does not consider previous interactions with the user when processing subsequent user inputs. Thus, a user may not be able to efficiently transfer their interactions with the machine learning model to another user and/or provide such interactions for subsequent processing. In addition, the context/knowledge available to the machine learning model may therefore be limited to the inputs provided by the user, resulting in reduced utility to the user.

It is with respect to these and other general considerations that aspects of the present disclosure have been described. Moreover, although relatively specific problems have been discussed, it should be understood that aspects disclosed herein should not be limited to addressing the specific problems identified in the background.

Disclosure of Invention

Aspects of the present disclosure relate to machine learning instantiation in which instances of conversational agents (e.g., including processing user inputs by a machine learning model to generate model outputs) are packaged as agent objects. In an example, the agent object is stored as a file, document, database, and/or the like. The agent object includes a role definition and/or an object embedded memory to define various aspects of the agent. Thus, the agent object allows portability of the session agent, e.g., between users, across contexts, and/or for various subsequent processes, etc.

This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form that are further described below in the detailed description. This summary is not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to be used to limit the scope of the claimed subject matter.

Detailed Description

In the following detailed description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof, and in which is shown by way of illustration specific aspects or examples. These aspects may be combined, other aspects may be utilized, and structural changes may be made without departing from the present disclosure. Aspects disclosed herein may be practiced as methods, systems, or devices. Accordingly, the disclosed aspects may take the form of a hardware implementation, an entirely software implementation, or an implementation combining software and hardware aspects. The following detailed description is, therefore, not to be taken in a limiting sense, and the scope of the present disclosure is defined by the appended claims and their equivalents.

In an example, a user interacts with a machine learning model, for example as a conversational agent that processes natural language input to generate model output accordingly. However, the user's interaction with the conversation agent may be limited to a conversational session, where a conversation history between the user and the conversation agent is maintained, and in some examples, at least a portion of the conversation history is provided as context to the machine learning model in generating the response. However, limiting machine learning model interactions to such simple chat-based paradigms may result in reduced portability (e.g., between scenes and/or across users) and/or may result in reduced utility to users, among other compromises. For example, users may not be able to efficiently export, share, or otherwise transfer their sessions with a conversation agent.

Accordingly, aspects of the present disclosure relate to machine learning instantiation in which instances of conversational agents (e.g., including processing user inputs by a machine learning model to generate model outputs) are packaged as agent objects. In an example, the agent object is stored as a file, document, database, and/or the like. As used herein, an agent object includes a role definition of the agent (e.g., including one or more hints for a machine learning model) and/or an object embedded memory, thereby defining various aspects of the agent. Additional examples of such aspects are discussed below, for example, with reference to fig. 2. Thus, the agent object allows portability of the session agent, e.g., between users, across contexts, and/or for various subsequent processes, etc.

For example, a user interacts with a conversation agent to define aspects of its role and/or to provide knowledge, context, or other information that may be used by the conversation agent. Thus, an instance of a conversation agent may be stored as an agent object (e.g., as a role definition and/or embedded in memory of the object) such that the agent object is used for subsequent processing. For example, the program code queries the agent object (e.g., using natural language and/or via an Application Programming Interface (API)) such that the agent object is used by the program code to generate model outputs and/or to retrieve information from a corresponding embedded object store.

As another example, the agent object is shared to other users (e.g., for collaboration and/or for subsequent use by other users). In another example, the agent object allows versioning such that various versions of the agent object have different associated properties (e.g., different roles and/or different embedded object stores). Thus, it should be appreciated that in some examples, the agent object implements semantics similar to those possible for a file or document (e.g., a file or document of a data store and/or online collaboration platform), such as saving the agent object, curing the agent object Long Zhineng, restoring the agent object to a previous state, creating a new version of the agent object, and/or managing rights for the agent object (e.g., according to an access control list). As another example, due to the portability of each session agent according to aspects described herein, one or more agent objects are used to virtualize the session agent with which they are associated.

In an example, the role definition and/or embedded object store of the agent object may be omitted and/or replaced, thereby forming a different agent object. For example, different agents (e.g., as defined by different roles) may be used to process the same embedded object store, thereby providing different agents with access to the information stored by the embedded object store. As another example, the same persona may be used to process different, additional, or less embedded object memory, thereby affecting the information that the persona is available to process. For example, embedded object memory from different agent objects may be provided to the agent defined by the initial agent object. As another example, a previous version of the embedded object store may be restored to allow the agent to "forget" for a period of time. As another example, at least a portion of the agent object may be used in conjunction with different models (e.g., of different versions and/or different types). For example, a first character definition of a first agent object associated with a first model may be used as a second character definition of a second agent object used in conjunction with a second model. Similarly, the first embedded object store of the first agent object may be used as a third embedded object store of a third agent object used in conjunction with a third model. In the case where an existing embedded object store is used by a different model, the embedded object store may be transformed or otherwise migrated from a previous model (e.g., a model associated with the existing embedded object store) to a new model such that the semantic vector of the migrated embedded object store corresponds to the different model accordingly. Thus, the role definition and/or embedded object store may be portable between models, enabling different ML processing to be performed (e.g., according to different models) based on similar roles and/or stores. Any of a variety of other actions may be performed with respect to the character definition, such as by merging characters, deduplication characters, and/or hydration/dehydration characters, among others.

As used herein, an embedded object store may store one or more semantic embeddings, each corresponding to one or more content objects. For example, a system hosting the model may provide information through a semantic context and may query an embedded object store (e.g., a vectorized command store) to find matching content information through semantic addresses and/or semantic proximity (e.g., using cosine distance or another geometric n-dimensional distance function). In some examples, the content object itself may be partitioned, sliced, and/or subdivided, for example, to allow finer granularity indexing and semantic proximity matching. This in turn may help discover useful overlaps, similarities, and/or cross-connections (edges) with other content objects.

The embedded object store may store the embeddings associated with the model and its particular version, which may represent the same content information in different semantic embedding spaces. When a new model is added, the content object may be re-encoded in the semantic space of the new model (e.g., by generating a new embedding) to add to the model set. In this way, a single content object may have a locatable semantic address in the cross-model. Storing and retrieving matching content objects may require specific methods to ensure that the content objects are available across models. The present disclosure discusses aspects of inserting an entry into an embedded object store, retrieving information from the embedded object store, and rebalancing the embedded object store.

In some examples, a hierarchy of a set of models may be constructed. For example, the hierarchy may be a tree, a graph, or another data structure of stored content. In some examples, not only may content objects be subdivided into finer-grained segments, but sets of related content objects (such as those related by subject matter, creation time, or other attributes recognized by one of ordinary skill in the art) may be aggregated. The aggregated content objects may form a more general higher level layer of the data structure, such as a tree. AI models, such as those described herein, can be used to create new aggregated or merged content (e.g., summary, annotation, rewrite, etc.) that captures the higher-level semantic meaning of the underlying collection into a single new object. The object may in turn be converted into an embedding.

Some aspects of the present disclosure relate to methods, systems, and media for storing entries in embedded object store. Typically, one or more content items (e.g., email, audio data, video data, messages, internet encyclopedia data, skills, commands, source code, programming evaluations, etc.) may be received. The one or more content items may include one or more content data (e.g., each email in an email, each audio file in audio data, each video file in video data, each message in a message, each page of an internet encyclopedia, etc.). One or more content data associated with the content item may be provided to one or more semantic embedding models (e.g., generative large language models, machine learning models, etc.) to generate one or more semantic embeddings. One or more semantic embeddings can be received from one or more semantic embedment models. In this regard, the large amount of information received by the computing device may be converted into embeddings that can be mathematically compared (e.g., semantic embeddings), and the amount of memory occupied by these embeddings is small relative to the large amount of information itself.

The set of semantic embeddings can be associated with a corresponding semantic embedment model. For example, the first set of embeddings can be associated with a first semantic embedding model of the one or more semantic embedding models. Further, the set of embeddings may include a first semantic embedment generated by the first semantic embedment model for at least one content data from the respective content item. In some examples, the semantic embedding model may be optimized for a particular scenario. For example, some semantic embedding models may be configured to produce an embedding with excellent results for semantic proximity of a particular object type, such as email (e.g., for a particular user and/or organization). As another example, some semantic embedding models may be configured based on a particular question type (e.g., looking up documents with 3-4 word topic digests that are relatively close based on semantic similarity). Semantic embedding models optimized for a particular scene may generate relatively smaller or relatively larger embeddings than other semantic embedding models not configured for the particular scene. In some examples, hints may be provided to the semantic embedding model, such as to configure the model for a particular scenario. The prompt may be provided by the user and/or by an automated system, such as to provide options or policies related to the input provided to the model.

One or more semantic embeddings received from the semantic embedding model can be inserted into the embedded object memory. The one or more semantic embeddings can be associated with respective indications corresponding to locations of source data associated with the one or more semantic embeddings. Furthermore, the insertion may trigger a spatial storage operation to store one or more semantically embedded vector representations. The vector representations may be stored in at least one of an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) tree, a k-dimensional (k-d) tree, an octree, an n-dimensional tree, or another data structure that one of ordinary skill in the art may recognize based at least on the teachings described herein.

Additionally or alternatively, some aspects of the present disclosure relate to methods, systems, and media for retrieving information from embedded object store. In general, an input embedding generated by a machine learning model may be received. Input embedding is discussed in further detail later herein. The stored embedded multiple sets may be retrieved by the mechanisms described herein. The embedded plurality of sets may each correspond to respective content data. At least one embedded subset may be retrieved from the stored plurality of sets of embeddings based on similarity to the input embeddings. Further, an action may be determined based on the subset of embeddings and the input embeddings.

In some examples, the embedded object store may contain tuples including stored embeddings, such as { value, embedded } or { key, embedded }. In such examples, the key, value, or identification of the original content associated with the embedding may be retrieved while the embedding remains within the memory. Thus, the closest embedding to the input may be found and the associated key, value, identification, and/or reference may be returned.

In some examples, the original content, such as from which the embedding was generated, may be discarded. If an automatic encoder is used to generate the embeddings, the original content can be approximately regenerated using a decoder given the encoding of the content (e.g., the embeddings).

Some scenarios in which the embedding itself may be retrieved may include, given a set of objects, desiring to create a centroid (average) representing the set of objects, and boundary coordinates surrounding the space in which the embedding of the set of objects is located. These scenarios may be used for object aggregation and index building.

Additional example aspects of embedded object memory are described in U.S. provisional patent application No.63/433,619 entitled "STORING ENTRIES IN AND RETRIVING INFORMATION FROM AN EMBEDDING OBJECT MEMORY (storing entries in embedded object memory and retrieving information from embedded object memory)", the entire disclosure of which is incorporated herein by reference for all purposes. Further, while examples are described herein with reference to embedded object stores, it should be understood that any of a variety of additional or alternative information may be stored as a store of session agents, including, but not limited to, session histories and/or documents, and the like.

Thus, a user may define and/or train an agent object for any of a variety of scenarios in accordance with aspects described herein. For example, an agent object may be created to provide customer support, for educational purposes (e.g., teaching a given subject area to one or more people), and/or for generating an article of manufacture according to aspects described herein. Further, different versions of such agent objects may be used (e.g., to provide support for different versions or to teach about different subject areas).

FIG. 1 illustrates an overview of an example system 100 that can perform machine learning instantiation in accordance with aspects of the present disclosure. As shown, the system 100 includes a machine learning service 102, a computing device 104, a computing device 106, and a network 108. In an example, the machine learning service 102, the computing device 104, and/or the computing device 106 communicate over a network 108, the network 108 may include a local area network, a wireless network, or the internet, or any combination thereof, or the like.

As shown, the machine learning service 102 includes a machine learning execution framework 110, an agent object processor 112, a model repository 114, and a data store 116. The agent object processor 112 is illustrated using a dashed box to indicate that in some examples, the agent object processor 112 may be omitted from the machine learning service 102. For example, the agent object processor 112 is included by the computing devices 104 and/or 106 to enable local processing of agent objects in accordance with aspects described herein. In other examples, machine learning service 102 includes agent object processor 112, while computing devices 104 and/or 106 omit agent object processor 120 and/or 124, which may be the case when one or more users of computing devices 104 and/or 106 cooperate on an agent object via machine learning service 102. Thus, it should be understood that any of a variety of paradigms are contemplated.

In an example, the machine learning execution framework 110 processes the user input to provide a model output in response (e.g., as may be generated using a machine learning model of the model repository 114) to provide a conversational agent with which a user of the computing device 104 and/or the computing device 106 may interact. While examples of user interaction with an agent are described, it should be understood that similar techniques may be used in instances where program code interacts with an agent, as well as other examples.

For example, processing the input to generate model outputs for a given conversational agent (e.g., of an agent object) may include processing the input according to an execution chain (e.g., having one or more model skills and/or programming skills). As used herein, an execution chain (also referred to as a skill chain) may include one or more sequential skills, a set of hierarchical skills, a set of parallel skills, and/or skills that rely on or otherwise process output from two or more skills, as well as other examples.

For example, model skills have associated hint templates for generating hints (e.g., including inputs and/or contexts) that are processed using the corresponding ML models to generate model outputs accordingly. In other examples, the ML model associated with model skills need not have an associated hint template, as is the case when ML models do not use hints when processing inputs to generate model outputs. As another example, the programmatic skills may read the content of the file, obtain data from a data source and/or from a user, send an electronic message containing the model output, create a file containing the model output, and/or execute the programmatic output generated by the model skills.

Thus, in instances where the machine learning execution framework 110 uses execution chains to process inputs, it may be possible to accomplish tasks and/or generate model outputs that would otherwise not be possible through a single machine learning model evaluation. For example, in processing a skill chain, information may be obtained from one or more data sources and/or input may be requested from a user and then used for subsequent processing (e.g., by one or more subsequent skills of the skill chain). As another example, the evaluation of the skill chain may be dynamically adapted as a result of the component evaluation, thereby affecting one or more future evaluations of the skill chain (e.g., by adding an evaluation, removing an evaluation, or changing an evaluation). Further, the execution chain itself may be managed, coordinated, and/or derived by the ML model (e.g., by generating the ML model based on natural language input received from a user and/or input generated by or otherwise received from an application). Additionally, given different ML models may be linked together (e.g., they may each generate different types of model outputs), the resulting model outputs may be output that would otherwise not result from the processing of a single ML model. Additional aspects of the machine learning execution framework 110 are described in U.S. provisional patent application No.63/433,627 entitled "Multi-stage machine learning model chain," which is incorporated herein by reference in its entirety for all purposes.

As another example, the agent object is provided for processing by a chain of execution (e.g., by a programming and/or machine learning block) such that the agent object is queried (e.g., using one or more natural language inputs) and/or information is extracted from a memory associated therewith, among other examples. In other examples, the agent object may be used as a skill that is processed as part of the execution chain. It should be appreciated that any of a variety of alternative or additional processes may be performed using the agent object, such as by program code executing on computing devices 104 and/or 106.

The machine learning service 102 is shown to further include a model repository 114, which may include any number of different machine learning models. For example, model repository 114 includes one or more base models, language models, speech models, video models, and/or audio models. As used herein, a base model is a model that is pre-trained on a wide range of data that can be adapted to a wide range of tasks (e.g., a model that is capable of handling a variety of different tasks or modalities). In an example, the multimodal machine learning model of the model repository 114 may be trained using training data having a plurality of content types. Thus, given a first type of content, the model of model repository 114 may generate content having any of a variety of associated types. It should be appreciated that model repository 114 may include a base model, as well as trimmed models (e.g., for a particular context and/or a particular user or group of users), and so forth.

As another example, a generative model (also referred to herein generally as a type of machine learning model) used in accordance with aspects described herein may generate any of a variety of output types (and thus may be a multimodal generative model in some examples), and may be a generative converter model and/or a Large Language Model (LLM), i.e., a generative image model, in some examples. Example Machine Learning (ML) models include, but are not limited to, a generative pre-training transducer 3 (GPT-3), a large open science open access multilingual language model (Big Science BLOOM), DALL-E, DALL-E2, stableDiffusion, or Jukebox. Additional examples of such aspects are discussed below with reference to the generative ML model shown in fig. 5A-5B.

The system 100 is shown as further comprising a data store 116 that can store one or more agent objects for subsequent retrieval (e.g., by the machine learning execution framework 110, the computing device 104, and/or the computing device 106). Additionally or alternatively, computing devices 104 and/or 106 include such data stores.

Referring now to computing device 104, computing device 104 further includes application 118 and agent object processor 120. In an example, the application 118 receives user input and provides model output, as may be generated by an agent object processor (e.g., agent object processors 112, 120, and/or 124) in accordance with aspects described herein. Aspects of the smart object processor 120 are similar to the smart object processors 112 and 124, such that the smart object processors 112 and 124 need not be described in detail.

In examples, the agent object processor 120 processes input according to agent objects to provide instances of agents with which users and/or program code may interact, as well as other examples. As described above, a machine learning model (e.g., a model of model repository 114) is used to generate model outputs, thereby providing instances of the agent accordingly. The agent object processor 120 processes the inputs according to roles defined by the agent objects and/or embedded object stores to generate model outputs accordingly. Additional examples of such aspects are discussed below with reference to fig. 2,3, and 4.

As shown, the system 100 includes two computing devices 104 and 106 such that a first user of the computing device 104 may share an agent object with a second user of the computing device 106. In an example, the first user sends the agent object in an electronic message, as the user may send a file or document in other ways. As another example, the first user stores the agent object at a location (e.g., data store 116) accessible to the second user. In such examples, an access control list or other set of permissions may be defined for the agent object such that the second user may be granted access to the agent object accordingly. As another example, the machine learning service 102 functions as a collaboration platform (or uses a separate collaboration platform) such that the first user and the second user can collaborate using the agent object through the machine learning service or the collaboration platform. It should be appreciated that other examples may include any number of computing devices and/or associated users.

FIG. 2 illustrates an overview of another example system 200 that can perform machine learning instantiation in accordance with aspects described in the present disclosure. As shown, the system 200 includes an agent object 202, an agent object processor 204, and a machine learning service 206. Aspects of the agent object processor 204 and the machine learning service 206 may be similar to the agent object processor 120 and the machine learning service 102 discussed above with reference to fig. 1, and thus need not be described in detail below.

The agent object 202 is provided as an example agent object defining aspects of a conversation agent in accordance with aspects described herein. As shown, the agent object 202 includes a persona 208 and an embedded object store 210. The agent object 202 is also shown to include roles 212 and embedded object store 214 to indicate that the agent object may include any number of roles and/or embedded object stores. Further, as described above, different roles and/or embedded object stores may be added, removed, or replaced to create new versions of an agent object or different agent objects, etc.

In an example, the persona 208 includes a set of cues that define or otherwise manage interactions of the agent. For example, roles 208 include description definitions, intent rewrite definitions, response generation definitions, and memory fetch definitions. Aspects of the persona 208 may be user-definable and/or may be hard-coded, as well as other examples. Moreover, it should be understood that in other examples fewer, alternative, and/or additional definitions may be used. For example, additional and/or alternative definitions may be used to define and/or simulate other aspects of meta-cognition and/or executive functions to create more complex roles for an agent.

As an example, the description definition includes a hint defining a personality of the agent. The intent rewrite definition may include a prompt to process an input to extract an intent associated therewith. In some instances, the extracted intent is used to identify a context associated with the intent, for example, from embedded object store 210. For example, it is intended to generate a feature vector from which one or more corresponding content objects are identified.

The response generation definition may include hints for generating model outputs for a given input. In an example, the hint also incorporates at least a portion of the input, a descriptive definition, and/or one or more content objects (e.g., as retrieved from embedded object store 210 according to intent associated with the given input). In some examples, the prompt further includes at least a portion of an interaction history with the agent. Thus, the response generation definition is used to generate a hint to generate the model output, where the hint includes a context that the machine learning model is available to when generating the model output.

The memory extraction definition may include hints for evaluating the input and/or corresponding model output to extract content, which may be stored for later retrieval (e.g., in embedded object memory) to record one or more interactions with the agent (e.g., for later retrieval based on intent with semantic similarity to the recorded content). In an example, the memory fetch definition specifies multiple types of memory (e.g., each type of memory may have an associated embedded object memory), such as short term memory, long term memory, and/or facts, among others. In some examples, the memory extraction definition includes an indication of a format of the corresponding model output such that the machine learning model is induced to generate a model output in accordance with the indicated format accordingly.

In an example, the agent object includes a hierarchy of roles and/or embedded object memory. For example, the user-defined role 208 loads the content side into the embedded object store 210 (e.g., as a natural language and/or as one or more embedded vectors) and dialogues with the agent defined by the agent object 202 to effectively train the agent about model outputs that should be generated from. In an example, the machine learning execution framework provides such functionality that enables content to be loaded into the embedded object store 210, such as by calling commands or as API calls, etc.

As an example, a user description (e.g., a novel or textbook) causes the agent to be used to generate the article accordingly. Example articles of manufacture include, but are not limited to, word processing documents, spreadsheets, websites, and/or presentation documents, and the like. In such an example, when talking to the agent, the user may focus on the various sub-portions of the book such that corresponding hierarchies are defined within the agent object 202 accordingly. Thus, when generating an article, a machine learning process may be performed based on one or more particular nodes of the hierarchy (e.g., nodes corresponding to sub-portions of the article). In examples, such nodes may be extended (e.g., with additional interactions of the user with the agent), split and/or merge, etc.

Thus, aspects of the agent object 202 are processed by the agent object processor 204 to produce an agent with which a user and/or program code can interact, among other examples. For example, the agent object processor 204 generates one or more machine learning process requests based on the roles 208/212 and/or embedded object stores 210/214, thereby causing the machine learning service 206 to generate model outputs for a given output in accordance with aspects described herein. Additional examples of these aspects are described below with reference to fig. 3 and 4.

FIG. 3 illustrates an overview of an example method 300 for providing a conversational agent based on agent objects, according to aspects described herein. In an example, aspects of method 300 are performed by an agent object processor (such as agent object processors 112, 120, and/or 124 in fig. 1 and/or agent object processor 204 in fig. 2).

As shown, the method 300 begins at operation 302, where user input is obtained. For example, the user input may be received by an application (e.g., application 118 and/or 122 in FIG. 1). Although examples are described with reference to input from a user, it should be understood that similar techniques may be used for input from program code and/or any of a variety of other sources. In an example, the input includes natural language input and/or any of a variety of other inputs.

At operation 304, the user input is processed to extract intent. For example, the input is processed according to the agent object's intent override definition, as described above with reference to agent object 202 in FIG. 2. In some examples, processing the input to extract the intent includes providing at least a portion of the indication of the input and the intent override definition to a machine learning model for processing (e.g., a machine learning model of the machine learning service 102 in fig. 1) such that the machine learning model generates a model output including the intent corresponding to the input.

Flow proceeds to operation 306 where the context is obtained from the embedded object store corresponding to the intent generated in operation 304. As an example, the extracted intent is used to generate feature vectors from which one or more content objects are retrieved from an embedded object store (e.g., of the agent object). While example memory storage and associated retrieval techniques are described, it should be appreciated that any of a variety of alternative or additional memory storage and/or retrieval techniques may be used in other examples.

At operation 308, an agent hint is generated based on the user input and the context. In an example, the agent hint is generated based on a response generation definition of the agent object. The response generation definition may be processed to generate an agent hint, which, as described above, may thus include at least a portion describing the definition (e.g., defining the personality of the agent), input, context from one or more content objects identified at operation 306, and/or at least a portion of the dialog history of the agent, among other examples.

Moving to operation 310, a model output is obtained based on the agent hint generated in operation 308. Similar to operation 304, the model output may be obtained by generating a machine learning model processing request that includes an agent hint such that the model output is received in response to the request. The request may be provided to a machine learning service (e.g., machine learning service 102 in fig. 1). Although examples are described herein with reference to a machine learning service, it should be understood that similar processing may alternatively or additionally be performed locally at a computing device of a user.

Flow proceeds to operation 312 where an indication of the model output is provided in response to the user input obtained at operation 302. For example, an application that obtains user input may display at least a portion of the model output. Although the method 300 is described in the example of a user interacting with an agent defined by an agent object, it should be appreciated that any of a variety of additional or alternative techniques may be used to provide model output. For example, in an instance in which input is obtained from the program code, the model output may be provided accordingly in response (e.g., a function call to a machine learning process) so that the model output may be further processed by the program code.

At operation 314, the embedded object store is updated based on the acquired input and/or the provided output. In an example, operation 314 is performed based on a memory fetch definition of the agent object, where the memory fetch definition includes a hint that induces a machine learning model to determine one or more instances of content to record. Fig. 5A and 5B illustrate an overview of an example generated machine learning model that may be used in accordance with aspects described herein. Referring first to fig. 5A, a conceptual diagram 500 depicts an overview of a pre-trained generative model package 504 that processes input 502 to generate model output for storing entries in embedded object memory 506 and/or retrieving information from embedded object memory 506 in accordance with aspects described herein. Examples of pre-trained generative model packages 504 include, but are not limited to Megatron-Turing natural language generative model (MT-NLG), generative pre-training transducer 3 (GPT-3), generative pre-training transducer 4 (GPT-4), bigScience BLOOM (large open science open access multilingual language model), DALL-E, DALL-E2, stableDiffusion, or Jukebox.

In an example, generative model package 504 is pre-trained according to various inputs (e.g., various human languages, various programming languages, and/or various content types), and thus does not require fine tuning or training for a particular scenario. Rather, generative model package 504 may be more generally pre-trained such that input 502 includes hints that are generated, selected, or otherwise designed to cause generative model package 504 to produce a particular generative model output 506. For example, the hint includes a context and/or one or more complement prefixes, thereby preloading the generative model package 504 accordingly. As a result, generative model package 504 is caused to generate an output based on the hint that includes the predicted sequence of tokens associated with the hint (e.g., reaching the token limit of generative model package 504). In an example, the predicted word sequence is further processed (e.g., by output decoding 516) to produce output 506. For example, each token is processed to identify a corresponding word, word segment, or other content that forms at least a portion of output 506. It should be appreciated that input 502 and generative model output 506 may each include any of a variety of content types, including, but not limited to, examples of text output, image output, audio output, video output, program output, and/or binary output. In an example, the input 502 and the generative model output 506 may have different content types, such as may occur when the generative model package 504 includes a generative multimodal machine learning model.

Thus, the generative model package 504 may be used in a variety of scenarios, and further, different generative model packages may be used in place of the generative model package 504 without substantial modification of other related aspects (e.g., aspects similar to those described herein with respect to fig. 1, 2, 3, and 4). Thus, the generative model package 504 is used as a tool to perform a machine learning process in which certain inputs 502 of the generative model package 504 are programmatically generated or otherwise determined, such that the generative model package 504 produces model outputs 506 that are subsequently available for further processing.

The generative model package 504 may be provided or otherwise used in accordance with any of a variety of examples. For example, the generative model package 504 may be used locally at a computing device (e.g., computing devices 104 and/or 106 in fig. 1) or may be accessed remotely from a machine learning service (e.g., machine learning service 102). In other examples, the distribution of generative model packages 504 is across multiple computing devices. In some instances, generative model package 504 may be accessible via an Application Programming Interface (API), such as an API that may be provided by the operating system of the computing device and/or by machine learning services, as well as other examples.

Referring now to the illustrated aspects of generative model package 504, generative model package 504 includes input tokenization 508, input embedding 510, model layer 512, output layer 514, and output decoding 516. In an example, input tokenization 508 processes input 502 to generate input embeddings 510 that include a sequence of symbolic representations corresponding to input 502. Thus, input embedding 510 is processed by model layer 512, output layer 514, and output decoding 516 to produce model output 506. An example architecture corresponding to generative model package 504 is depicted in FIG. 5B, which is discussed in further detail below. Even so, it should be understood that the architectures shown and described herein are not to be considered limiting, and in other examples any of a variety of other architectures may be used.

FIG. 5B is a conceptual diagram depicting an example architecture 550 of a pre-trained, generated machine learning model that may be used in accordance with aspects described herein. As noted above, any of a variety of alternative architectures and corresponding machine learning models may be used in other examples without departing from the aspects described herein.

As illustrated, architecture 550 processes input 502 to generate generative model output 506, aspects of which are discussed above with respect to fig. 5A. Architecture 550 is depicted as a converter model including an encoder 552 and a decoder 554. Encoder 552 processes an input insert 558 (aspects of which may be similar to input insert 510 in fig. 5A) that includes a sequence of symbologies corresponding to input 556. In an example, the inputs 556 include the inputs 502 corresponding to machine learning blocks of the execution chain.

In addition, position encoding 560 may introduce information regarding the relative and/or absolute position of the lemma of input insert 558. Similarly, output insert 574 includes a sequence of symbologies corresponding to output 572, and position code 576 may similarly introduce information regarding the relative and/or absolute position of the lemma of output insert 574.

As shown, encoder 552 includes an example layer 570. It should be understood that any number of such layers may be used, and that the depicted architecture is simplified for illustrative purposes. The example layer 570 includes two sub-layers, a multi-headed attention layer 562 and a feed-forward layer 566. In an example, a residual connection is included around each layer 562, 566, followed by normalization layers 564 and 568, respectively.

The decoder 554 includes an example layer 590. Similar to encoder 552, any number of such layers may be used in other examples, and the depicted architecture of decoder 554 is simplified for illustrative purposes. As shown, the example layer 590 includes three sub-layers, a mask multi-head attention layer 578, a multi-head attention layer 582, and a feed forward layer 586. Aspects of the multi-headed attention layer 582 and the feedforward layer 586 may be similar to those discussed above with respect to the multi-headed attention layer 562 and the feedforward layer 566, respectively. In addition, the masked multi-head attention layer 578 performs multi-head attention on the output (e.g., output 572) of the encoder 552. In an example, the masked multi-headed attention layer 578 prevents a location from focusing on a subsequent location. Such masking in combination with offset embedding (e.g., offset by one location, as shown by multi-headed attention layer 582) may ensure that the prediction for a given location depends on the known output of one or more locations that are smaller than the given location. As shown, residual connections are also included around layers 578, 582 and 586, followed by normalization layers 580, 584 and 588, respectively.

Multiple head attention layers 562, 578, and 582 may each linearly project queries, keys, and values to corresponding dimensions using a set of linear projections. Each linear projection may be processed using an attention function (e.g., dot product or additive attention) to produce an n-dimensional output value for each linear projection. The resulting values may be concatenated and projected again such that the values are then processed as shown in fig. 5B (e.g., by the corresponding normalization layer 564, 580, or 584).

The feed forward layers 566 and 586 may each be a fully connected feed forward network applied to each location. In an example, the feed forward layers 566 and 586 each include a plurality of linear transformations with linear cell activation of the correction therebetween. In an example, each linear transformation is identical at a different location, and different parameters may be used compared to other linear transformations of the feed forward network.

In addition, aspects of the linear transformation 592 may be similar to the linear transformations discussed above with respect to the multi-headed attention layers 562, 578, and 582 and the feed forward layers 566 and 586. Softmax (normalized exponential function) 594 may also convert the output of linear transformation 592 to a predicted next labeling probability, as shown by output probability 596. It should be appreciated that the illustrated architecture is provided as an example, and in other examples, any of a variety of other model architectures may be used in accordance with the disclosed aspects. In some cases, multiple iterations of the process (e.g., using the generative model package 504 in fig. 5A or the encoder 552 and decoder 554 in fig. 5B) are performed according to the above aspects to generate a series of output tokens (e.g., words), e.g., which are then combined to produce a complete sentence (and/or any of a variety of other content). It should be appreciated that other generation models may generate multiple output tokens in a single iteration, and thus may use a reduced number of iterations or a single iteration.

Thus, according to aspects described herein, the output probabilities 596 may thus form the ML outputs 506 for the agents defined by the agent objects such that the output to generate the ML model may be provided as model outputs for the agents that are responsive to the inputs to the agents accordingly.
